questions.q: A quiz team prepares three statements about the Rigveda for a round. (a) 'The Rigveda has 1,028 hymns, and every one of them praises a deity.' (b) 'Historians agree on the exact date when the Rigveda was composed.' (c) 'Vedic literature was passed on orally for several centuries before it was written down.' Check (a), (b) and (c) against the chapter, say whether each is right or wrong, and correct it if it is wrong. (d) The team wants to explain to the audience why the corrected fact in (b) is so. Using your answer to (c), give one reason why historians must treat the date of the Rigveda with care.
questions.a: (a) Wrong in part: the Rigveda does have 1,028 hymns (suktas), but only some praise deities; others reflect on universal thoughts such as creation and cessation, birth and death. (b) Wrong: the date of composition is debated among historians, with estimates ranging from the fifth millennium BCE to the second millennium BCE. (c) Right: Vedic literature existed in oral form for several centuries before it was written down. (d) Because the hymns were passed on orally for centuries, the written copies come from much later than the time the hymns were composed, so the date of composition cannot be read from them and has to be estimated; this is why the estimates range so widely.
s: (a) Wrong: 1,028 hymns, but some praise deities and others reflect on creation, birth and death
(b) Wrong: the date is debated, fifth to second millennium BCE
(c) Right: oral for several centuries before being written
(d) Oral transmission means the written text is much later than its composition, so the date must be estimated and stays debated

questions.q: Arjun writes in his notes: 'Around 600 BCE northern India had only kings, never republics. In the Deccan the Mauryas were followed by the Satavahanas. The early Chola, Chera and Pandya kingdoms of the Sangam age are the same as the imperial kingdoms of later centuries.' Check each of his three sentences against the chapter: say whether it is right or wrong, and correct any that is wrong.
questions.a: First sentence wrong: northern India then had both monarchical states (rajyas) and republican states (ganas or samghas). Second sentence right: in the Deccan the Mauryan Empire was succeeded by the Satavahana Empire, which lasted nearly 500 years. Third sentence wrong: the chapter warns that these early kingdoms should not be confused with the later imperial Chola, Chera and Pandya kingdoms that emerged many centuries later.
s: Sentence 1 wrong: both rajyas (monarchies) and ganas or samghas (republics)
Sentence 2 right: the Satavahanas succeeded the Mauryas in the Deccan (nearly 500 years)
Sentence 3 wrong: the early kingdoms are not the later imperial kingdoms, which came many centuries later

questions.q: A newly crowned king hears three advisers. Adviser A: 'Rule alone; councils only slow a king down.' Adviser B: 'Judge the strong and the weak alike and protect the land from calamities.' Adviser C: 'Rest in the palace; your officers will work whatever you do.' Using the chapter: (a) Judge Adviser A's advice. (b) Judge Adviser B's advice. (c) Judge Adviser C's advice. (d) Explain why Kautilya would also warn the king to look after all seven constituents together. (e) Which adviser should the king follow? Justify in one line.
questions.a: (a) Poor advice: the king did not rule alone but governed through a multi-layered administration with a council of ministers (mantri-parishad) to advise him; the Arthashastra says 'one wheel does not move the carriage'. (b) Sound advice: it matches the coronation oath of the Yajurveda, which asks the king to judge the strong and weak impartially and fairly and to protect the country from all calamities. (c) Poor advice: the Arthashastra says only if the king is himself energetically active do his officers follow him energetically. (d) Kautilya saw the state as an organic whole of seven constituents, which can function effectively only if they remain properly integrated. (e) Adviser B, because his advice alone agrees with the king's duties of justice and protection described in the chapter.
s: (a) A rejected: king governed with a council of ministers; 'one wheel does not move the carriage'
(b) B accepted: Yajurveda oath of impartial justice and protection from calamities
(c) C rejected: officers are energetic only if the king himself is energetically active
(d) State is an organic whole; works only if the seven constituents are integrated
(e) Chooses B with a reason tied to justice and protection

questions.q: A student's chart of administrative units between 300 CE and 800 CE reads: North - province: bhukti; division: vishaya; district: vithi. South - province: mandalam; division: kottam; district: pattala. Check the chart against the chapter and correct the entries that are wrong.
questions.a: In the north, bhukti (province) and vishaya (division) are right, but vithi is wrong as a district: vithis were groups of villages, and northern districts were adhishthana or pattana. In the south, mandalam (province) and kottam (division) are right, but pattala is wrong as a district: southern districts were nadu, while pattala and kurram were groups of villages.
s: North: bhukti and vishaya right; south: mandalam and kottam right
North district wrong: adhishthana or pattana, not vithi (a group of villages)
South district wrong: nadu, not pattala (a group of villages)

questions.q: A history club compares the records of three southern villages. Village 1, under the Pallavas (c. 275-897 CE), received land free of tax from the king. Village 2, under the Chalukyas of Badami (c. 543-753 CE), was a Brahmin settlement at Aihole that slowly became a well-known centre of learning. Village 3, under the imperial Cholas, chose the members of its own committees in the 10th century. (a) What does the chapter call villages like Village 1, and settlements like Village 2? (b) For how many years in all, by these dates, did the Pallava dynasty last? (c) Name the method by which Village 3's committees were chosen, and the inscription that describes it. (d) The club concludes that the records of all three villages show villages running their own affairs. Do the three villages' own records, as described here, support this? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Village 1 is a Brahmadeya village; Village 2 is an agraharam. (b) 897 - 275 = 622 years. (c) The Kudavolai or ballot-pot system: names of eligible candidates were written on palm leaves, put in a pot and drawn by a young child; it is known from the Uttaramerur inscription of Parantaka I. (d) Only partly: Village 3's record shows a village choosing its own committees, but the records of Villages 1 and 2 show only a tax-free royal land grant and a Brahmin settlement that became a centre of learning, which say nothing about self-government, so the claim holds for Village 3 alone.
s: (a) Brahmadeya village; agraharam
(c) Kudavolai (ballot-pot) system; Uttaramerur inscription of Parantaka I
(d) Partly: holds for Village 3; Villages 1 and 2 show royal grants and a learning centre, not self-government

questions.q: Rohan says, 'Rita in the Rigveda is only about the movement of nature, like the sun and the rain; it has nothing to do with how people behave.' Using the chapter, show why he is only partly right.

s: Agrees in part: rita regulates the forces of nature
Corrects him: rita is order and balance in human society too and upholds moral values

questions.q: A newspaper column claims: 'Rulers in early India cared only about conquest. Ethics was a matter for priests and sages, never for kings or village councils.' A student collects evidence from the chapter to reply. She notes that Ashoka's edicts spoke of moral conduct, respect within the family, non-violence and compassion; that a 10th-century inscription set conditions for candidates in village elections; and that some literary works gave advice on kingship. She also notes that the Chola ruler Rajendra I took the title Gangaikonda. (a) Name the idea that Ashoka's edicts promoted, and its Sanskrit equivalent. (b) Name the 10th-century inscription and the two conditions it set for candidates. (c) Name two literary works that, according to the chapter, contain advice on kingship and governance. (d) Does the evidence support the column? Judge, taking the Gangaikonda title into account.
questions.a: (a) Dhamma, the Pali equivalent of the Sanskrit word dharma. (b) The Uttaramerur inscription; candidates should have 'honest earnings' and be 'pure' of mind. (c) Kamandaka's Nitisara and Banabhatta's Kadambari. (d) Only partly: rulers did seek conquest, as Rajendra I's title Gangaikonda for his conquests along the Ganga shows, but the chapter shows a link between politics and ethics from the Mauryas to the Cholas, so the claim that ethics was never a concern of kings or councils is wrong.
s: (a) Dhamma, Pali equivalent of dharma
(b) Uttaramerur inscription: honest earnings and pure of mind
(c) Kamandaka's Nitisara and Banabhatta's Kadambari
(d) Partly: conquest was sought (Gangaikonda), but ethics guided rulers and councils from the Mauryas to the Cholas, so 'never' is wrong

questions.q: A school exhibition panel is titled 'Women in Early India: Only Homemakers?'. Using the chapter: (a) Name the Gupta princess who ruled as a regent in the Vakataka kingdom, and say what she issued in her own name. (b) Name two Sangam poetesses. (c) Name two economic tasks that Sangam literature shows women performing. (d) Name the Chola royal woman whom inscriptions record as a supporter of temple building. (e) The chapter also says that over time women's position fluctuated and even declined. Analyse whether the panel's title question should be answered 'yes' or 'no', using (a) to (d).
questions.a: (a) Prabhavati Gupta, daughter of Chandragupta II; she issued land grants in her own name. (b) Avvaiyar and Vennikuyattiyar. (c) Any two of planting, weeding, husking and winnowing paddy, cattle rearing, spinning, fishing, salt production and garland selling. (d) Sembiyan Mahadevi. (e) 'No': although women's position fluctuated and even declined over time, women continued to act in governance (a regent issuing grants), literature (poetesses), the economy (agrarian and craft work) and religious patronage (temple building), so they were far more than homemakers.
s: (a) Prabhavati Gupta; issued land grants in her own name
(b) Avvaiyar and Vennikuyattiyar
(c) Two economic tasks such as planting, winnowing paddy, spinning, fishing, salt making
(d) Sembiyan Mahadevi
(e) Answers 'no': despite decline, women acted in governance, literature, economy and patronage

questions.q: Match each work in Column I with the field of the literary heritage of early India it belongs to in Column II. Column I: 1. Panini's Ashtadhyayi  2. Tiruvalluvar's Tirukkural  3. Yajnavalkya Smriti  4. Sushrutasamhita. Column II: (a) classical works on medicine  (b) smriti literature on dharma, law and ethics  (c) foundational texts for Sanskrit grammar  (d) Tamil literature
(a) Name any two personal deities around whom worship came to be centred as the Vedic tradition evolved. (b) In which century and region did the organised Bhakti tradition gain prominence?
questions.a: (a) Any two of Vishnu, Shiva and Shakti. (b) In the 6th century, in the Tamil region, through the Alvars and Nayanmars.
s: (a) Any two of Vishnu, Shiva, Shakti
(b) 6th century, Tamil region

questions.q: Read the passage. Kavya's class is studying how students learnt in early India. The chapter says that the teacher's home was the centre of the gurukula, and the student was treated as a member of the teacher's family. Students studied the Vedas along with grammar, logic, philosophy, ethics, mathematics, science, medicine and astronomy. They were also trained in music, dance, painting, physical education and martial arts such as archery, and practised yoga and meditation. (a) What was the centre of the gurukula? (b) Name two subjects studied in a gurukula. (c) Name two arts or crafts in which students were trained. (d) According to the chapter, how was the teacher-student relationship (guru-shishya parampara) regarded, and how was the teacher seen?
questions.a: (a) The teacher's home. (b) Any two of the Vedas, grammar, logic, philosophy, ethics, mathematics, science, medicine and astronomy. (c) Any two of music, dance, painting, physical education and archery. (d) The relationship was regarded as sacred, and the teacher was highly respected as a guide who helped students move from the darkness of ignorance to the light of knowledge.
s: (a) The teacher's home
(b) Two subjects such as the Vedas, grammar, mathematics, astronomy
(c) Two arts such as music, dance, painting, archery
(d) Regarded as sacred; the teacher a respected guide from the darkness of ignorance to the light of knowledge

questions.q: Assertion (A): The Vedic people viewed nature not merely as a resource but as sacred and powerful. Reason (R): Each Vedic deity was associated with an element of nature, and early societies depended on nature for survival. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Check each of these three claims against the chapter and say whether it is right or wrong, with a reason. (a) 'The Vedic pantheon had a fixed order with one god always ranked above all others.' (b) 'The centres of higher learning in early India were meant only for students from within India.' (c) 'Using the chapter's timeline, Nalanda university was established about half a century before Vallabhi university.'
questions.a: (a) Wrong: the Vedic pantheon did not follow a rigid hierarchy, and different deities are praised as supreme in different hymns. (b) Wrong: institutions of higher learning attracted students from both India and other regions. (c) Right: Nalanda was established in 427 CE and Vallabhi in 480 CE, and 480 - 427 = 53 years, about half a century.
s: (a) Wrong: no rigid hierarchy; different deities supreme in different hymns
(b) Wrong: students came from India and other regions
(c) Right: 427 CE and 480 CE, 53 years apart

questions.q: (a) Name two crops whose cultivation Sangam texts vividly describe. (b) Name the standard Sanskrit lexicon that has a special chapter on forest, crops, plants and manure.
questions.a: (a) Ragi and sugarcane. (b) The Amarakosha.
s: (a) Ragi and sugarcane
(b) Amarakosha

questions.q: A Mauryan revenue officer visits a village to assess its land. (a) Name any three types of village land that Kautilya describes. (b) The village has 240 acres of land in all. Of this, 30 acres are groves and 50 acres are pasture; the rest is cultivated. How many acres are cultivated? (c) Where in the village were its groves found? (d) The state cleared forests to expand farming. What does the chapter say about some forests?
questions.a: (a) Any three of cultivated land, wasteland or fallow land, high and dry land, sown fields and groves. (b) 240 - 30 - 50 = 160 acres. (c) On the outskirts of the village. (d) Certain categories of forests were protected by law.
s: (a) Any three of cultivated, waste or fallow, high and dry, sown fields, groves
(c) On the village's outskirts
(d) Certain categories of forests were protected by law

questions.q: A class project is titled 'Guilds of early India'. Answer each part in one or two lines. (a) What were guilds (shrenis)? (b) Name two ways in which guilds protected artisans and consumers. (c) Which form of money came into circulation in the same period, after the rise of the mahajanapadas, and which coins came first? (d) Name any two kinds of textiles that literary and archaeological sources refer to. (e) Name three centres that emerged as important hubs of textile production.
questions.a: (a) Associations of people engaged in the same profession, craft or occupation, such as traders, artisans and merchants. (b) They regulated the quality of goods and often fixed prices. (c) Metallic coins, beginning with silver punch-marked coins. (d) Any two of silk, cotton, wool and linen. (e) Mathura, Kashi and Kamarupa.
s: (a) Associations of people of the same profession, craft or occupation
(b) Regulated quality and fixed prices
(c) Metallic coins, beginning with silver punch-marked coins
(d) Two of silk, cotton, wool, linen
(e) Mathura, Kashi, Kamarupa

questions.q: The Milindapanho describes eight stages of agricultural operations, from preparing and weeding the fields to harvesting and winnowing. (a) What does this show about farming in the post-Mauryan period? (b) Why does the chapter call agriculture the backbone of the economy?
questions.a: (a) It shows a detailed understanding of farming practices. (b) Because agriculture sustained both rural livelihoods and the revenue of the state.
s: (a) A detailed understanding of farming practices
(b) It sustained both rural livelihoods and state revenue

questions.q: A trader from Magadha in the Mauryan age plans a long journey. He will carry goods along a major land route to the Deccan and then to a port on the coast. Before he leaves, he wonders how the state will help merchants like him on the way. (a) Name two goods that, according to the Arthashastra, Magadha traded with other parts of India. (b) Name the two major land routes that had emerged by about the 6th century BCE. (c) Give two things the state did, as described in the chapter, that would help this trader and his buyers. (d) Name two major ports of early India, and explain how such routes and ports together helped trade.
questions.a: (a) Any two of textiles, gems, coral, pearls, metals and minerals. (b) Dakshinapatha and Uttarapatha. (c) The state ensured the safety of trade routes, took measures to prevent adulteration of goods and protect consumers from unfair practices, and strictly regulated salt production. (d) Any two of Muziris, Kaveripattinam, Arikamedu and Masulipatnam; the routes connected inland regions with coastal ports, integrating overland and maritime trade.
s: (a) Two of textiles, gems, coral, pearls, metals, minerals
(b) Dakshinapatha and Uttarapatha
(c) Two state measures: safe routes, no adulteration and consumer protection, regulated salt
(d) Two ports and the link of inland routes with coastal ports

questions.q: The assembly of a 10th-century Chola village can afford only one project. Plan 1: dig a connecting channel from the village tank to 40 acres of new fields; each acre would give 300 kg of grain, but only in years when the tank fills, which happens in about four years out of five. Plan 2: build a market shed for passing traders, which would bring the village income worth 9,000 kg of grain every year. (a) Name three kinds of irrigation works, besides connecting channels, that the Cholas built. (b) How much grain would the new fields give in a year when the tank fills? (c) Over five years, compare the total from Plan 1 with the total from Plan 2. (d) Give two ways in which, according to the chapter, irrigation structures like this helped a region. (e) Which plan should the assembly choose? Justify with your numbers and one point from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Canals, lakes and tanks. (b) 40 x 300 = 12,000 kg. (c) Plan 1: 12,000 x 4 = 48,000 kg; Plan 2: 9,000 x 5 = 45,000 kg; Plan 1 gives 3,000 kg more. (d) Any two of: they stored and distributed water, supported agriculture and encouraged the growth of settlements. (e) Either plan, if justified with the five-year totals and one chapter point. For example: Plan 1, the channel, because even counting the dry year it gives 3,000 kg more over five years, and irrigation supports agriculture and helps settlements grow; or Plan 2, the shed, because its 9,000 kg comes every year while the channel gives nothing in a dry year and is ahead by only 3,000 kg (about 6%), and the chapter notes the growing importance of trade.
s: (a) Canals, lakes, tanks
(c) 48,000 kg against 45,000 kg; channel ahead by 3,000 kg
(d) Two of: store and distribute water, support agriculture, encourage settlements
(e) Chooses a plan and justifies it with the five-year totals (channel ahead by 3,000 kg on average; shed steadier) and one chapter point
